name: Nivea Creme blue tin

card.summary: A classic multipurpose moisturising cream in a blue tin, used on dry skin on the face, hands and body to keep skin soft and smooth.
card.note: Contains lanolin-based emulsifier; people sensitive to lanolin may react.

quick.overview:
Nivea Creme is a thick water-in-oil moisturiser sold in a blue tin with a white logo. People use it on dry skin of the face, hands and body to keep skin soft and smooth-looking.

It launched in 1911 and the tin dates from 1925, and it is reported as a long-lived household staple.
quick.how: Applied to skin, for example after a shower, as one forum user described using Nivea on dry patches of arms and shoulders in winter.[2]
quick.risks: Contains lanolin-derived emulsifier, so people with sensitivity to lanolin may react. Product details differ by market.

lead: Nivea Creme is a moisturising cream from the German company Beiersdorf, introduced in 1911 and described as the first stable water-in-oil emulsion.[1] It is sold in a blue tin with a white logo adopted in 1925.[1]
People use it to keep dry skin soft and smooth, such as on arms and shoulders in winter, as a T Nation poster described in 2003.[2]

The cream relies on Eucerit, a lanolin-based emulsifier patented in 1900 by Isaac Lifschutz, which Oscar Troplowitz and dermatologist Paul Gerson Unna helped bring into the product.[1] No published trial has tested the tin product itself.

angle.text: It moisturises dry skin on the face, hands and body, which leaves skin looking smoother. Users apply it as a basic everyday cream.

paras: Paul Beiersdorf founded the company in 1882 and pharmacist Oscar Troplowitz took over in 1890.[1] Nivea soap came in 1906 and Nivea Creme in 1911.[1] The cream was relaunched in the blue tin in 1925.[1]
Forum users describe it as a post-shower moisturiser for dry patches, in one case alongside a hand cream for cracking skin.[2]
